questions.stem: The conception of privacy proposed by Warren and Brandeis is modeled most closely on:

options.A: an owner's right to exclude others from property
options.B: a contract between a citizen and the press
options.C: the public's right to be informed about private citizens
options.D: a state's duty to protect citizens from crime

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage says its model was property, as a person may exclude trespassers from a house. Why the others are wrong: B) No contract is mentioned. C) The press prompted the argument but the right protects individuals against it. D) Crime prevention is a concern of surveillance defenders, not of this conception.
questions.trap: Taking the newspapers that provoked the right as its model.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates the harm of aggregation described in the passage?

options.A: A neighbor reads a single postcard that a visitor has left lying open on a hallway table.
options.B: A data broker combines harmless purchases and locations to infer that a customer is ill.
options.C: A camera records a person once as she crosses a public street on her way to work.
options.D: An employer reads an email that a colleague addressed directly to him about a project.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says harm emerges from combining items, none of which reveals much alone. Why the others are wrong: A) A single item read in a private setting is intrusion rather than aggregation. C) A single recording in public is the discrete item the traditional doctrine considers. D) Reading mail addressed to oneself involves no combination.
questions.trap: Choosing a single invasive act, which is the harm the property view already covers.

questions.stem: Which finding would most directly support the chilling effect described in the third paragraph?

options.A: After a surveillance program expands, crime rates fall in the monitored neighborhoods over several years.
options.B: Users accept lengthy data policies without reading them, because the service would otherwise be unavailable.
options.C: People who share more personal data online report greater satisfaction with the services they use.
options.D: After publicity about monitoring, users search less for controversial topics though they broke no law.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The chilling effect is a change in behavior by people who believe they are watched, even with nothing to hide. Why the others are wrong: A) A fall in crime concerns security, not the behavior of law-abiding people. B) Accepting policies relates to consent, not to avoiding unpopular activity. C) Greater satisfaction is unrelated to changes in behavior under observation.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about consent when the question is about behavior change.

questions.stem: Under Nissenbaum's account, which scenario would most clearly be a privacy violation?

options.A: A patient describes his symptoms to a doctor in order to receive treatment.
options.B: A woman tells a friend over dinner about her own illness.
options.C: A teacher reads a student's essay aloud at the student's request.
options.D: A pharmacy sells customers' prescription records to a marketing firm.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Medical information moves to a setting whose norms do not allow it, which is an inappropriate flow. Why the others are wrong: A) The flow from patient to doctor matches the norms of that context. B) A person sharing her own information with a friend follows the norms of friendship. C) The student requested the reading, so the flow fits the purpose of sharing.
questions.trap: Treating any disclosure of sensitive information as a violation regardless of context.

questions.stem: Which of the following best exemplifies the weakness of the contextual account that the author notes?

options.A: A doctor shares a patient's record with an employer in violation of well-established medical norms.
options.B: A new platform's users disagree about whether a post may be reposted, and no norm exists.
options.C: A company states plainly in a notice, before the sale, exactly how it will use customers' data.
options.D: A court cannot decide a case because the facts of the dispute remain unresolved.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says a new technology may create a setting for which no norms exist, leaving the theory with little to say. Why the others are wrong: A) A clear violation of established norms is the kind of case the theory handles well. C) A plain notice does not involve the absence of norms. D) A dispute about facts is not a lack of norms.
questions.trap: Selecting a hard case about facts instead of one about missing norms.
